text_paragraph_1: I n every developing economy, the debate over where to place the nation’s scarce cedis is the ultimate test of economic wisdom. Recently, the Member of Parliament for Nhyiaeso, Dr. Stephen Amoah , sparked a vital national conversation when he questioned the innovation behind the government’s flagship "Big Push" infrastructure programme. His central argument—that building roads is a routine duty of governance rather than a groundbreaking economic breakthrough, and that Ghanaians are yearning for policies they can immediately feel in their pockets—strikes at the heart of our daily reality. Yet, as basic economics teaches us, producing food without reliable roads only breeds post-harvest waste and artificial scarcity. To truly lower food prices and uplift household incomes, Ghana must move beyond political slogans and strike a deliberate, well-sequenced balance between major highways, rural feeder roads, and direct agricultural support.

text_paragraph_1: South Sudan is at serious risk of returning to widespread armed conflict amid escalating political and security tensions. On 22 September 2026 President Salva Kiir dissolved the Transitional Government of National Unity (TGoNU), removed the vice presidents, ministers and local administrators and dissolved the national and state assemblies. He then appointed a caretaker administration to govern until elections, which were scheduled for 22 December 2026, but have subsequently been postponed to 11 February 2027. The attack triggered retaliatory actions by the SSPDF and a campaign of arrests targeting leaders aligned with First Vice President Riek Machar’s Sudan People’s Liberation Army-In Opposition (SPLA-IO), culminating in Machar’s placement under house arrest. title: ILO stand ready to help Rwanda put the wage commitments of its new employment policy into practice
text_paragraph_1: KIGALI (ILO News) – Government, employers’ and workers’ representatives met in Kigali on 8 October 2026 for a high-level social dialogue on minimum wage, part of the national consultations on Rwanda’s draft National Employment Policy (NEP) 2026–2036, supported by the Government of Luxembourg and the European Union. Organized by the Ministry of Public Service and Labour (MIFOTRA) with ILO support, the dialogue brought together the Permanent Secretary of MIFOTRA, the Chief Executive Officer of the Private Sector Federation (PSF) and the President of the Centrale des Syndicats des Travailleurs du Rwanda (CESTRAR), alongside ILO experts.
text_paragraph_2: The draft NEP shifts the focus from the number of jobs to their quality. Rwanda created some 2.08 million jobs between 2017 and 2025, but around 90 per cent of them are informal. The draft therefore commits to guidelines for a sector-by-sector minimum wage determination process and to strengthening the National Labour Council as the primary mechanism for the progressive determination and review of wage policies. The question now is how to turn these commitments into a process that is credible, evidence-based and jointly owned.
text_paragraph_3: The ILO presented what international labour standards, notably the Minimum Wage Fixing Convention, 1970 (No. 131) offer on this question. They do not prescribe a figure. They describe how to reach one: equal participation of employers and workers, a balance between the needs of workers and their families and economic factors, regular review and effective application. He also outlined the choices before Rwanda, including which workers to cover, whether to adopt a national floor, sectoral rates or both, how to phase in and review changes, and how to ensure compliance, including through the NEP’s digital payroll and registration tools. The dialogue was technical in nature and did not involve the determination of minimum wage rates. Participants considered what evidence each party would need to trust the outcome and what first steps the National Labour Council could agree over the next 12 months.

text_paragraph_1: Rwanda has emerged as one of Africa's strongest performers in anti corruption controls, public administration and budget management, according to the 2026 Ibrahim Index of African Governance. Yet the same assessment places the country 49th in media freedom and records deterioration in political participation, civil society space and institutional checks. The contrasting results raise questions about the relationship between administrative efficiency, independent scrutiny and the institutions that protect public resources, particularly as Rwanda seeks to attract international investment and expand its regional economic influence.
text_paragraph_2: Rwanda ranks joint first among Africa's 54 countries in anti corruption performance but 49th in media freedom, according to the 2026 Ibrahim Index of African Governance (IIAG) released by the Mo Ibrahim Foundation on October 31, 2026, presenting one of the continent's clearest contrasts between administrative governance and the institutional conditions for independent public scrutiny. The country scored 76.6 out of 100 in Anti Corruption, sharing the continental lead with Seychelles, while its Media Freedom indicator stood at 29.7 after declining by 12.6 points between 2016 and 2025. During the same period, Rwanda improved its Public Administration score by 6.3 points, reaching 77.7 and ranking fifth in Africa, while its wider Participation, Rights & Inclusion category deteriorated by 4.9 points.
text_paragraph_3: The findings are particularly relevant to Rwanda's economic model, which has attracted international attention for the organisation of public institutions, administrative coordination, investment facilitation and enforcement of government policies. Rwanda ranked 14th in overall governance in 2025, scoring 58.9 out of 100, an improvement of just 0.4 points compared with 2016. That relatively modest overall change conceals substantial differences between the country's underlying indicators. Foundations for Economic Opportunity improved by 2.7 points to 63.7, while Human Development increased by 3.6 points to 65.1. Participation, Rights & Inclusion, however, fell to 42.0, and Rights declined by 5.8 points to 31.5. The difference raises an institutional question with consequences extending beyond politics: how should the effectiveness of government administration be assessed when the mechanisms through which journalists, civil society organisations and citizens independently scrutinise public decisions record weaker results?

source: Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect
text_paragraph_1: Populations in the Central Sahel – Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger – are enduring armed conflict and inter-communal violence amidst an entrenched and expanding insurgency driven by armed Islamist groups affiliated with al-Qaeda (JNIM) and the so-called Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP). Violence has also taken place between rival ethnic militias and community-based self-defense groups resulting in reprisal attacks and countless abuses. There have been thousands of conflict-related civilian deaths, including 2,640 recorded by the UN between January and March 2026.
text_paragraph_2: Armed Islamist groups perpetrate recurrent abuses and attacks against civilians. These groups systematically use sieges, threats, kidnappings, improvised explosive devices, drones and landmines as deliberate tactics of war as they seek to control supply routes and increase areas of influence. They have increasingly consolidated control along major transport corridors, isolating communities through blockades, disrupting markets and restricting civilian movement, including in urban areas. In besieged areas, armed Islamist groups are blocking humanitarian aid to civilians and causing starvation, imposing forced taxation and strategically destroying and looting civilian objects, including places of worship, health centers, food reserves and water services, among other violations of International Humanitarian Law (IHL). They have also enforced their own interpretation of Sharia law in areas under their control, imposing severe gender discriminatory rules. Insurgents also routinely perpetrate grave violations against children and target secular state education, burning schools and threatening, abducting or killing teachers.
text_paragraph_3: Counterterrorism operations have often led to human rights violations in all three states, with security forces in Mali and Burkina Faso implicated in likely war crimes and crimes against humanity. The Malian Armed Forces (FAMa) and Russian state-controlled Africa Corps (formerly the Wagner Group) have perpetrated possible war crimes and crimes against humanity, including summary executions, indiscriminate airstrikes, rape and sexual violence, pillaging and torture against civilians, among other abuses. State-sponsored militias in Burkina Faso, notably the Volunteers for the Defense of the Homeland (VDP), have also been implicated in grave crimes along ethnic lines. According to Human Rights Watch, the ethnic targeting of Fulani civilians by the Burkinabè military and VDPs through killings, enforced disappearances and looting, which resulted in the mass displacement of entire communities, amounts to ethnic cleansing.

text_paragraph_1: Despite slight improvements from the previous IPC analysis, acute food insecurity in Lebanon remains widespread across all population groups and is particularly severe among refugees and recently displaced Lebanese populations. Household-level evidence continues to show severe pressures on livelihoods, purchasing power and coping capacity, while livelihoods, purchasing power and household resilience remain severely constrained. The improvement compared to the previous analysis also reflects a reduction in the overall population of Syrian refugees. Between September 2026 and February 2027, approximately 1.05 million people, representing 21 percent of the analysed population, are experiencing IPC Phase 3 or above (Crisis or worse), including 52,000 people in Emergency (IPC Phase 4) and approximately 997,000 people in IPC Phase 3 (Crisis).
text_paragraph_2: The situation is driven by the cumulative impacts of two consecutive conflicts in less than two years, compounded by a fragile economic environment and rising living costs. While the October 2025 IPC analysis reflected the impact of the 2023–2024 conflict and subsequent ceasefire, the current analysis assesses food security outcomes following a second major conflict escalation that began in March 2026. Although the intensity of the conflict has decreased since the June 2026 ceasefire agreement, the security situation remains fragile, with hostilities continuing in southern Lebanon despite ongoing diplomatic efforts to secure a more durable ceasefire. This prolonged insecurity has further undermined households’ capacity to recover from previous losses, displacement, livelihood disruptions, and asset depletion.
text_paragraph_3: Food insecurity in Lebanon is increasingly shaped by deteriorating livelihoods and constrained economic access to food. Although markets remain functional and food is generally available across most areas of the country, households face significant constraints in accessing it due to weak income opportunities and reduced purchasing power. The combined effects of conflict-related livelihood losses, slow reconstruction, elevated food and fuel prices, and rising transportation and energy costs continue to erode households’ economic access to food. As food prices remain elevated and incomes fail to recover at the same pace as living costs, many households continue to rely on debt, consumption-based and livelihood coping strategies, and humanitarian food security assistance (HFSA) to meet their basic food needs. The cumulative impact of these drivers has reduced households’ ability to absorb further shocks, particularly among vulnerable Lebanese households, refugees, agricultural communities, displaced populations, and residents of conflict-affected areas.

text_paragraph_1: South Sudan is at serious risk of returning to widespread armed conflict amid escalating political and security tensions. On 22 September 2026 President Salva Kiir dissolved the Transitional Government of National Unity (TGoNU), removed the vice presidents, ministers and local administrators and dissolved the national and state assemblies. He then appointed a caretaker administration to govern until elections, which were scheduled for 22 December 2026, but have subsequently been postponed to 11 February 2027. The postponement further delays the political transition and heightens the risk of continued instability.
text_paragraph_2: The electoral framework itself raises additional concerns. Under amendments to the 2012 National Elections Act, Kiir will retain full presidential and constitutional powers throughout the electoral period. The amendments also removed the previous requirements to complete a permanent constitution and conduct a national census before elections could be held.
text_paragraph_3: The dissolution follows a prolonged erosion of the political process established under the 2018 Revitalized Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in South Sudan (R-ARCSS), which ended the country’s 2013-2015 civil war and intended to establish a path towards stability. Fighting between forces aligned with Kiir – the South Sudan People’s Defence Forces (SSPDF) – and armed opposition groups flared in February 2025 after opposition groups overran an army base in Nasir. The attack triggered retaliatory actions by the SSPDF and a campaign of arrests targeting leaders aligned with First Vice President Riek Machar’s Sudan People’s Liberation Army-In Opposition (SPLA-IO), culminating in Machar’s placement under house arrest. By March 2025 these developments had effectively rendered the power-sharing framework inoperative, signaling the broader collapse of the political settlement.

source: Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect
text_paragraph_1: Populations in the Central Sahel – Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger – are enduring armed conflict and inter-communal violence amidst an entrenched and expanding insurgency driven by armed Islamist groups affiliated with al-Qaeda (JNIM) and the so-called Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP). Violence has also taken place between rival ethnic militias and community-based self-defense groups resulting in reprisal attacks and countless abuses. There have been thousands of conflict-related civilian deaths, including 2,640 recorded by the UN between January and March 2026.
text_paragraph_2: Armed Islamist groups perpetrate recurrent abuses and attacks against civilians. These groups systematically use sieges, threats, kidnappings, improvised explosive devices, drones and landmines as deliberate tactics of war as they seek to control supply routes and increase areas of influence. They have increasingly consolidated control along major transport corridors, isolating communities through blockades, disrupting markets and restricting civilian movement, including in urban areas. In besieged areas, armed Islamist groups are blocking humanitarian aid to civilians and causing starvation, imposing forced taxation and strategically destroying and looting civilian objects, including places of worship, health centers, food reserves and water services, among other violations of International Humanitarian Law (IHL). They have also enforced their own interpretation of Sharia law in areas under their control, imposing severe gender discriminatory rules. Insurgents also routinely perpetrate grave violations against children and target secular state education, burning schools and threatening, abducting or killing teachers.
text_paragraph_3: Counterterrorism operations have often led to human rights violations in all three states, with security forces in Mali and Burkina Faso implicated in likely war crimes and crimes against humanity. The Malian Armed Forces (FAMa) and Russian state-controlled Africa Corps (formerly the Wagner Group) have perpetrated possible war crimes and crimes against humanity, including summary executions, indiscriminate airstrikes, rape and sexual violence, pillaging and torture against civilians, among other abuses. State-sponsored militias in Burkina Faso, notably the Volunteers for the Defense of the Homeland (VDP), have also been implicated in grave crimes along ethnic lines. According to Human Rights Watch, the ethnic targeting of Fulani civilians by the Burkinabè military and VDPs through killings, enforced disappearances and looting, which resulted in the mass displacement of entire communities, amounts to ethnic cleansing.

text_paragraph_1: The University of Southern Denmark (SDU) made waves when its research ethics committee (REC) voted to approve a controversial vaccine clinical trial set to take place in Guinea-Bissau. The October approval led to renewed international criticism despite a revised protocol from the lead investigators at the SDU-affiliated Bandim Health Project. The trial caught the attention of the Bissau-Guinean government and, following a local police search and seizure of vaccines from the Bandim offices, was canceled .
text_paragraph_2: However, questions remain as to how and why the SDU REC gave assent to this study. RECs, the European equivalent of American institutional review boards (IRBs), are university-run interdisciplinary academic panels that evaluate the ethics behind studies that involve human subjects. They have the power to reject planned studies outright or ask for revisions to the protocol. Critics allege that the proposed vaccine study failed at the first hurdle when it comes to the critical question of equipoise , arguing it should never have received the go-ahead from a REC or IRB.
text_paragraph_3: In order to explore this question further, BioXconomy sought views from two experts on clinical trials: Arthur Caplan, an American medical ethicist and professor emeritus at New York University Grossman School of Medicine, and Boghuma Titanji, a clinical researcher and physician from Cameroon and an associate professor at Emory University in Atlanta, Georgia. We also spoke with Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding REC member who resigned in protest along with half of the REC membership following the vote.

text_paragraph_1: Botswana's economy grew 8.7 percent year on year in the second quarter of 2026, while output outside mining slipped 0.2 percent and manufacturing contracted 9.2 percent. That uneven recovery explains why President Duma Gideon Boko's November 18 meeting with African Development Bank Group President Sidi Ould Tah in Abidjan matters. Botswana can post strong growth when mining recovers, yet still struggle to develop other industries and create jobs. The partnership's economic test is whether it helps Botswana's firms sell a wider range of goods and services, at home and abroad.
text_paragraph_2: Boko outlined a plan for a digitally enabled, export-led economy with more employment opportunities for women and young people. Ould Tah said the bank was ready to support mineral processing, industrial production and participation in regional supply chains. The visit reaffirmed those priorities and highlighted a $503.75 million loan that the bank's board had already approved in October to help Botswana absorb an energy shock and advance economic reforms.
text_paragraph_3: Botswana's dependence on diamonds makes export earnings and public finances sensitive to demand for a single commodity. The International Monetary Fund has identified weak natural diamond demand as a reason to diversify and pointed to persistently high youth unemployment as a constraint on broad-based growth. The second-quarter figures show how those problems can persist through a headline recovery. Stronger mining output lifted GDP while manufacturing weakened and real household consumption fell 7.3 percent year on year.

text_paragraph_1: The union’s Deputy CEO, Robert Rabasimane, said they will consider escalating the matter to international organisations to prevent the country from being greylisted. Last week Thursday, Minister of Higher Education Prince Maele, standing in for Leader of the House, Moeti Mohwasa, revealed in Parliament that Moti has been granted citizenship by investment, a flagship brought by the UDC government upon assuming power. “The proprietor (Moti) of African Hero, who was the representative developer of the school and the clinic, has been granted citizenship by investment after meeting the necessary requirements in terms of Section 10 of the Citizenship Act,” Maele told Parliament. The minister indicated that the Duma Boko School and clinic in Block 7 was a first, as the plan is to build 100 more schools and clinics, a five-star hotel at Gaborone Dam, chrome mining and has already been given land in Gabane. Not taking that lying down, the Manual Workers union berated government for its decision to grant Moti citizenship. Rabasimane questioned whether Moti was even vetted. “Moti is not a suitable candidate for our citizenship,” Rabasimane told a media briefing yesterday.
text_paragraph_2: “As per our laws of this country, he does not deserve the citizenship of this country, as we heard Prince Maele as he defended the decision by government.” He added it is quite cumbersome to see Maele defending the decision to grant Moti citizenship by acting oblivious to facts before them. “It is embarrassing for Maele to state that there is no conflict of interest when it comes to Moti, who is a UDC investor and that is clear. “We even saw that he built a school at Block 7 and he said he built it because of his friend who is also President,” Rabasimane noted with concern. The unionist further said it is clear as day that Moti is favoured ahead of other potential investors. “There is conflict of interest and Moti is held up on a high accord and so many of our laws are bypassed when it comes to him and we won’t accept this as Manual Workers Union,” he added. Despite Maele indicating that Boko exercised his powers under Section 10 of the Citizenship Act, Rabasimane believes that his argument was flawed. “Maele read Section 10 of the Immigration Act and it was clear that he did not understand it. “Had he read it with an understanding and together with the Financial Intelligence Act (FIA) applied here, especially Sections 2 and 22, it clearly shows a person of Moti who has a questionable background, so the vetting was not done properly,” Rabasimane said. He further questioned how citizenship by investment is processed in Botswana, suggesting it does not follow international standards at all. “We are also shocked that this citizenship by investment is not a new thing in other countries, but the way it’s done here, we are not following it properly, it only favours our friends,” he said. “They are just taking Moti’s words, nothing has been put on the table. It is only promises and he might not even deliver on those promises.” Taking all these issues into consideration, Rabasimane said he harbours fears that bilateral relations might be tainted and, to avert that, they might escalate the issue. “This will dent our diplomatic relations with other countries. We don’t want to be greylisted and we might take this to international organisations to intervene,” Rabasimane added.

text_paragraph_1: Despite slight improvements from the previous IPC analysis, acute food insecurity in Lebanon remains widespread across all population groups and is particularly severe among refugees and recently displaced Lebanese populations. Household-level evidence continues to show severe pressures on livelihoods, purchasing power and coping capacity, while livelihoods, purchasing power and household resilience remain severely constrained. The improvement compared to the previous analysis also reflects a reduction in the overall population of Syrian refugees. Between September 2026 and February 2027, approximately 1.05 million people, representing 21 percent of the analysed population, are experiencing IPC Phase 3 or above (Crisis or worse), including 52,000 people in Emergency (IPC Phase 4) and approximately 997,000 people in IPC Phase 3 (Crisis).
text_paragraph_2: The situation is driven by the cumulative impacts of two consecutive conflicts in less than two years, compounded by a fragile economic environment and rising living costs. While the October 2025 IPC analysis reflected the impact of the 2023–2024 conflict and subsequent ceasefire, the current analysis assesses food security outcomes following a second major conflict escalation that began in March 2026. Although the intensity of the conflict has decreased since the June 2026 ceasefire agreement, the security situation remains fragile, with hostilities continuing in southern Lebanon despite ongoing diplomatic efforts to secure a more durable ceasefire. This prolonged insecurity has further undermined households’ capacity to recover from previous losses, displacement, livelihood disruptions, and asset depletion.
text_paragraph_3: Food insecurity in Lebanon is increasingly shaped by deteriorating livelihoods and constrained economic access to food. Although markets remain functional and food is generally available across most areas of the country, households face significant constraints in accessing it due to weak income opportunities and reduced purchasing power. The combined effects of conflict-related livelihood losses, slow reconstruction, elevated food and fuel prices, and rising transportation and energy costs continue to erode households’ economic access to food. As food prices remain elevated and incomes fail to recover at the same pace as living costs, many households continue to rely on debt, consumption-based and livelihood coping strategies, and humanitarian food security assistance (HFSA) to meet their basic food needs. The cumulative impact of these drivers has reduced households’ ability to absorb further shocks, particularly among vulnerable Lebanese households, refugees, agricultural communities, displaced populations, and residents of conflict-affected areas.

As food prices remain elevated and incomes fail to recover at the same pace as living costs, many households continue to rely on debt, consumption-based and livelihood coping strategies, and humanitarian food security assistance (HFSA) to meet their basic food needs. The cumulative impact of these drivers has reduced households’ ability to absorb further shocks, particularly among vulnerable Lebanese households, refugees, agricultural communities, displaced populations, and residents of conflict-affected areas.

Violence has also taken place between rival ethnic militias and community-based self-defense groups resulting in reprisal attacks and countless abuses. There have been thousands of conflict-related civilian deaths, including 2,640 recorded by the UN between January and March 2026.
text_paragraph_2: Armed Islamist groups perpetrate recurrent abuses and attacks against civilians. These groups systematically use sieges, threats, kidnappings, improvised explosive devices, drones and landmines as deliberate tactics of war as they seek to control supply routes and increase areas of influence. They have increasingly consolidated control along major transport corridors, isolating communities through blockades, disrupting markets and restricting civilian movement, including in urban areas. In besieged areas, armed Islamist groups are blocking humanitarian aid to civilians and causing starvation, imposing forced taxation and strategically destroying and looting civilian objects, including places of worship, health centers, food reserves and water services, among other violations of International Humanitarian Law (IHL). They have also enforced their own interpretation of Sharia law in areas under their control, imposing severe gender discriminatory rules. Insurgents also routinely perpetrate grave violations against children and target secular state education, burning schools and threatening, abducting or killing teachers.
text_paragraph_3: Counterterrorism operations have often led to human rights violations in all three states, with security forces in Mali and Burkina Faso implicated in likely war crimes and crimes against humanity. The Malian Armed Forces (FAMa) and Russian state-controlled Africa Corps (formerly the Wagner Group) have perpetrated possible war crimes and crimes against humanity, including summary executions, indiscriminate airstrikes, rape and sexual violence, pillaging and torture against civilians, among other abuses. State-sponsored militias in Burkina Faso, notably the Volunteers for the Defense of the Homeland (VDP), have also been implicated in grave crimes along ethnic lines. According to Human Rights Watch, the ethnic targeting of Fulani civilians by the Burkinabè military and VDPs through killings, enforced disappearances and looting, which resulted in the mass displacement of entire communities, amounts to ethnic cleansing.

What Happens to Western Sahara After the UN Mission Ends?
text_paragraph_1: The UN Security Council’s failure to renew MINURSO ends a 35-year peacekeeping mission and leaves the territory’s future uncertain.
text_paragraph_2: One of the United Nations’ longest-running peacekeeping missions abruptly ended last month after the UN Security Council (UNSC) rejected two competing draft resolutions from the US and Russia. Now, the future of Western Sahara, a former Spanish colony under Moroccan occupation since 1975, hangs in the balance. Some experts argue that it sets a “dangerous precedent” for other self-determination struggles around the world.
text_paragraph_3: The United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO by its French acronym) was established in 1991 to maintain a ceasefire between Moroccan forces and the Polisario Front, a political-military movement that represents the indigenous Sahrawi people. Spain’s hasty withdrawal from its former colony in 1975 led to a 16-year war over the territory, which is rich in natural resources including phosphates used in fertilizer. The mission was also tasked with carrying out a referendum for self-determination for the Sahrawi people, and had been consistently renewed by the Security Council — until now. In its draft resolution, the US proposed renaming MINURSO and removing the referendum from its mandate, affirming that “genuine autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty is the only feasible solution to the question of Western Sahara.” The US representative to the UN, Mike Waltz, said the US would not lend its support to “a mission whose very name perpetuates something that cannot be done.” Russia vetoed this text, arguing that it marginalized the Polisario and went against UN parameters for self-determination. Russia proposed a one-year technical rollover which also failed to secure the Council’s support. The mission expired on Oct. 31 as a result.
